s: Part three.
Distributing tools, and tool choice.
By the end of this part, you'll be able to tell apart three levers that people run together.
You'll know what goes in each agent's toolbag.
And you'll know which tool_choice value fits which job.
Two separate questions hide inside this task statement.
The exam pulls them apart, because practitioners run them together.
The first question.
What goes into someone's toolbag before they leave for the job?
The second.
Do you insist they come back with a completed form?
Take the first one.
A plumber called out for a dripping tap doesn't carry the whole van up the stairs.
And the reason isn't the weight.
Rummaging costs time.
And two spanners that look alike get picked wrong under pressure.
An agent has the same failure mode.
And it has none of the instincts a person uses to recover.
So you pack each agent a bag.
It holds what that job needs, and nothing else.
The second question stands apart.
Having settled what's in the bag, you can still say one of three things.
"Do not come back without the inspection sheet."
Or "use your judgment."
Or "today I want an answer in words and you touch nothing."
That's about one visit.
And it changes nothing about which tools are in the bag.
In exam terms, these are two of three separate levers.
One.
Distribution decides which tools an agent has.
Two.
Permission decides which calls run without asking a person.
Three. tool_choice decides whether the model may answer without calling a tool, on this particular request.
Confusing them is a reliable way to pick a distractor.
And here's the foundational fact.
Every registered tool costs context, and adds a candidate to every selection decision.
Accuracy degrades with tool count long before the context window fills.
Why?
Because near-duplicate descriptions collapse into each other.
First concept.
Shrinking the candidate set.
Picture a help desk where one person answers every question from a wall of twenty-eight binders.
And they keep grabbing the wrong one.
Merge the three binders that are always read together into one.
Give order questions and letter-writing to two different people, with their own shelves.
The wrong grabs mostly stop.
Question one.
This one is select two.
Here's the scenario.
A customer support coordinator has twenty-eight tools, across billing, orders, shipping, and outbound messages.
It picks the wrong tool about one turn in six.
Three of them, get_order_header, get_order_lines and get_order_payments, are called in that order on nearly every order question.
Which two changes are best?
Take a second.
The answers.
First, consolidate those three into a single order_details tool.
Second, split the work into an order agent and a messaging agent, each with an allowlist of only its role's tools.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: set tool_choice to any on every turn.
Why?
It makes the agent call something on every turn, including turns where it should just summarise.
And it doesn't help it choose.
Wrong: raise the maximum turn count.
Why?
That just lets it make more wrong calls.
Wrong: a table in the system prompt mapping intents to tool names.
Why?
It patches catalog ambiguity with instructions.
And selection still happens against twenty-eight tools.
The notes give a ranking for a crowded catalog.
Four steps.
First.
Consolidation.
Because removing a candidate removes the ambiguity outright.
Second.
Distribution.
Because it shrinks the set each agent sees.
Third.
Description and name repair.
Because it only makes the remaining candidates distinguishable.
And last.
Deferred loading.
Because it cuts context cost without fixing overlap.
Now, you may notice that sounds different from part one.
There, fixing the description came first.
So how do you tell which ladder you're on?
In part one, the stems described two or three tools with vague or overlapping wording.
And they asked for the first, or lowest-complexity, step.
So: fix the words.
Don't add architecture to solve a language problem.
Here, the stem describes a big catalog serving several roles, with tools that are always called together.
Removing and redistributing candidates is the structural fix.
Both ladders agree on one thing.
Architecture never fixes a labelling problem.
And labels never fix a catalog that's simply too big for one agent.
Hold on to this line.
Fewer candidates per agent beats better instructions about many candidates.
Second concept.
Allowlists versus denylists.
Picture an editor who's meant to polish an article.
But they keep leaving the office to interview new people.
Telling them to stop rarely sticks.
Handing them only a red pen and the draft keeps them editing.
Taking away just their phone still leaves the notebook in their pocket.
Now the technical detail.
In Claude Code, a subagent declares its tools in the frontmatter, at the top of its definition file.
The tools field is an allowlist.
If you omit it, the subagent inherits everything available.
That's rarely right for a specialist.
The disallowedTools field is a denylist.
When both are set, disallowedTools applies first.
Then tools resolves against what remains.
So a tool named in both is removed.
Both accept server-level patterns.
That's mcp__ followed by a server name.
Or that, plus a trailing star, for all of its tools.
And in disallowedTools, the pattern mcp__ followed by a star removes every M C P tool from every server.
Question two.
Here's the scenario.
A synthesis agent inherits every tool the coordinator has, including web_search and fetch_url.
Instead of writing up the findings it was handed, it launches new searches.
That blows its budget, and adds unverified sources.
It still needs verify_fact, to check claims.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
A tools allowlist containing verify_fact and what synthesis needs.
And nothing that gathers new sources.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: set disallowedTools to web_search.
Why?
That's a denylist over an inherited pool.
And denylists fail by omission. fetch_url stays granted.
And any research tool added later silently arrives.
Wrong: set tool_choice to none.
Why?
It blocks verify_fact along with everything else. tool_choice controls whether a call is allowed on a request, not which tools the agent has.
Wrong: a prompt instruction not to research.
Why?
It's a request, not a guarantee.
The notes give the same lesson from the security side.
A reviewer subagent is meant to be read-only.
It has disallowedTools set to Write.
Yet it keeps modifying files.
Why?
Denying Write leaves Edit.
And it leaves Bash, which can write files through any subprocess.
The fix is an allowlist, such as Read, Grep and Glob.
And if the agent truly needs a shell?
Know this.
Claude Code's read and edit deny rules cover only the file commands it recognises inside Bash.
Not a Python or Node script that opens files itself.
An operating-system-level sandbox is the only enforcement that covers every process.
Now a name collision to guard against, because the exam likes it.
There are three "allowed tools" settings.
And they do different things.
One. allowed-tools, with a hyphen.
It lives in a skill or slash command's frontmatter.
It pre-approves the listed tools, for that invoking turn only.
It restricts nothing.
Two. tools, in subagent frontmatter.
It restricts.
A tool left out is not in that agent's session at all.
Three. allowedTools, in camel case.
It's a software development kit option and command-line flag.
It permits.
It decides which calls run without a prompt.
So check the spelling in the question before you answer.
Hold on to this line.
Allowlists close the bag by construction.
Denylists forget things.
Third concept.
Putting a whole server where it's used.
Picture a plumber's entire van of tools being carried into every flat on the job.
Including the flats where only the electrician is working.
Everyone trips over it.
Leave the plumbing kit with the plumber, and the corridor clears for everyone else.
Question three.
Here's the scenario.
A team registers an incident-management M C P server, with forty-five tools, in the project's shared configuration.
Only the incident-triage subagent uses it.
But every developer's main session now carries those forty-five definitions.
And the main agent's tool selection has become less accurate.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Remove the server from the shared configuration.
And declare it in the triage subagent's own mcpServers field.
The notes call this the sharpest instrument in the task statement.
Why?
Because it moves the capability and its context cost together, into the one agent that needs both.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: turn on deferred tool loading.
Why?
It trims the context cost.
But it leaves the capability in the wrong agent.
Wrong: a line in the project CLAUDE.md file telling the main agent to ignore those tools.
Why?
It removes neither the forty-five candidates, nor their cost.
Wrong: move the server into each triage engineer's user-scope configuration.
Why?
That makes it private per machine.
So the team loses a shared, versioned definition.
Now deferred loading itself.
And here, the sources disagree.
The notes describe it as current behaviour.
Claude Code can defer M C P tool definitions, instead of loading them all upfront.
And Claude loads the schemas it needs through a tool called ToolSearch.
A whole server can opt out, with alwaysLoad set to true.
A single tool can opt out, with anthropic/alwaysLoad set to true in its _meta field.
The Developer Platform has a sibling, the tool search tool.
The lesson eight slide deck, however, says tools cannot be loaded lazily.
So how do you handle it?
Two rules.
If a question offers deferral as an option, treat it as real, and rank it last.
It cuts context cost.
But it doesn't make two indistinguishable descriptions distinguishable.
And it quietly rewards a catalog nobody cleaned up.
If a question frames lazy loading as a restriction, answer in the question's terms.
Hold on to this line.
Declare the server inside the one agent that needs it.
Defer only what genuinely has to stay large.
Fourth concept. tool_choice.
That's the form you insist they bring back.
Picture a council office.
It tells visitors they must leave with one of three forms filled in.
And each person picks the one that matches their errand.
Insisting everyone fills in the parking form would be wrong for most of them.
Merely asking nicely means some people chat at the counter, and leave with nothing.
There are four values.
One. auto.
It lets the model decide whether to call anything.
It's the default when tools are supplied.
Two. any.
It forces a tool call, but lets the model pick which.
Three. tool, together with a name.
It forces that one named tool.
Four. none.
It blocks tool calls on that request.
It's the default when no tools are supplied.
And a companion setting, disable_parallel_tool_use, reads differently per mode.
Under auto, it means at most one call, and text is still allowed.
Under any or tool, it means exactly one call.
Question four.
Here's the scenario.
A document-intake pipeline has three extraction tools. record_invoice, record_receipt, and record_purchase_order.
The document type is only known after the model reads the file.
With tool_choice on auto, about one response in ten is a prose summary the ingestion step cannot parse.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer. any.
It forces a tool call, while leaving the choice of schema to the model.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: tool, with the name record_invoice, because invoices are most common.
Why?
It forces the invoice schema onto receipts and purchase orders.
Wrong: auto, plus a prompt instruction.
Why?
It still permits a text-only answer.
And that's the reported failure.
Wrong: none, with all three schemas pasted into the prompt.
Why?
It forbids tool calls entirely, and falls back to unvalidated JSON in prose.
That's the least reliable option.
Now the contrast.
And a second source disagreement.
The notes have a mirror-image question.
An analytics agent must produce one strictly shaped record, called record_finding, at the end of each investigation.
And one run in eight ends in prose.
There, the best answer is tool, with the name record_finding, plus disable_parallel_tool_use.
Because a single schema is the deliverable.
Why does any lose in that item?
Because with more than one tool registered, the model can satisfy the constraint by calling the wrong tool.
The lesson seven deck puts it more simply.
It says to use any to guarantee structured output.
The notes prefer naming the tool.
Both guarantee a tool call.
The difference is whether they guarantee the right one.
So here's the rule.
When several schemas are acceptable, and the model must pick, choose any.
When one schema is the deliverable, name it.
Read the stem for how many acceptable outputs there are.
Two more tool_choice traps.
Wrong: set any on every request in an agentic loop, to make the agent more decisive.
Why?
On a turn where it should summarise, it calls something anyway.
It re-fetches data it has, or reaches for the nearest match.
That inflates turns, and risks loops.
The right shape is auto for the loop. any or tool for the one request that produces the artifact.
And optionally none on the final summarisation turn, so the model cannot start a new chain.
Wrong: use none to suppress one misbehaving tool.
Why?
It disables every tool on that request.
And forcing a call is also never a fix for a bad description.
It guarantees a call, not the right one.
That's part three.
Hold on to this line. auto to explore, any when several forms are acceptable, the named tool when one form is the deliverable, none to wrap up.
Coming up in part four: integrating M C P servers into Claude Code and agent workflows.
